Ford's Michigan LFP shipments shift battery demand toward lithium, while the Hawaii ruling clouds US seabed leasing. Gold's fall below $3,800 squeezes juniors.

sections: Industry health

Labour and permits, not prices, now set the pace of new supply. Highland Valley is in its fourth week with a replacement-worker order in place, and a BC court has reversed a consultation shortcut, so new tonnes are arriving later than the desk assumed.

Gold's slide below US$3,800 squeezes juniors first while majors such as Agnico keep spending above US$3.5bn. Chinese premiums and Codelco's 2027 premium cut both look like sales pushes, not shortages.
Regional trends

North America: Canada's federal money is going to tungsten (up to C$14M for Mactung, plus funding for the Yukon project), a defence-linked policy bet that means years before tonnes. US seabed leasing is now clouded by the Hawaii ruling, and a restored Boundary Waters moratorium is a proposal whose odds the midterm result may have raised.

Africa: Kenya's award of a large critical-minerals contract to a US consortium and Zimbabwe's lithium export-tax change with a local-sourcing mandate both show resource nationalism rising as critical minerals gain strategic value.

Latin America: Codelco's dust-permit threat in Chile is a reminder that operating permits are live risks, and El Niño water and power stress in Peru would likely show up first as higher costs before any output loss.
Technology & demand

Ford's Michigan LFP cells, built on CATL technology, take demand from nickel and cobalt and add to lithium, iron and phosphate. The shift is now production, but North American battery supply depends on a Chinese licensor.

Electrification, which the IEA says the Hormuz crisis has accelerated, adds copper and lithium demand over time, while sodium-ion and solid-state efforts trim long-run lithium and nickel demand but remain early. Transformer shortages are the nearer copper-related bottleneck, and data centres still reach copper only through grids.
On the horizon
A signed Highland Valley deal is the swing event. Restart would follow over weeks to months, so a signature alone would not add 2026 tonnes.
The Hawaii appeal and the US deep-sea lease sale. A government appeal can be filed up to 60 days after judgment, so a filing may come after mid-December and would still be ordinary.
Trump says the US will "see what happens" with Iran after January 1. Hormuz disruption would raise diesel and sulphur costs for North American and Chilean operations before it touched metal output.
creative: Sulphur is the hidden link between Hormuz and metal supply. Sulphuric acid is used in copper solvent extraction and electrowinning in Chile, and in high-pressure acid leach nickel projects in Indonesia, so a sulphur squeeze could raise costs in both places before any sanctions or shipping limits are felt. (speculation level: medium)

If labour is the binding constraint, the mines that gain most over the next five years may be those that automate haulage and maintenance and so need fewer hires per tonne. That would favour scale operators and could widen the gap with juniors. (speculation level: high)

Mongolia's presidential resignation and the Mongolia–Kyrgyzstan joint-project talks could make Oyu Tolgoi's policy terms a test case for how governments reopen contracts when political leadership changes. (speculation level: medium)
global_view:
The Trump, Xi and Putin summit around APEC produced a "peace declaration," and headlines disagree on what it achieved: some call it historic, others say the summit was "hijacked." The trade truce is described as "in flux." For mining, a calmer US-China trade track lowers tariff risk on copper flows, but the minerals licence terms are not in the headlines, so the desk's antimony, tungsten and rare-earth test is still open. Tighter TSMC chip curbs and warnings about AI regulation show that AI policy is moving fast, but data centres still reach mining through grids and power rather than directly.

Trump says the US will "see what happens" with Iran after January 1. That is the date to watch for Hormuz risk, which would raise diesel and sulphur costs for North American and Chilean operations before it touched metal output. Ukraine remains the source of munitions demand that holds up tungsten and antimony money. Putin has ruled out a Black Sea or energy truce, so that demand is not fading. The IMF warns global debt is nearing 100% of GDP, which tightens government budgets for critical-minerals programmes and junior financing. The Fiji drought disaster and the El Niño alert point to water and power stress in the Andes and Australia.

discussions.strategist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
Copper is the soft spot. The price has fallen below $13,000 while smelters chase supply, and the AI-linked sell-off has made the demand story harder to read. The binding constraints are still people and logistics. The Highland Valley strike is in its fourth week, and Teck has been barred from using newly promoted supervisors, so the fight is about replacement work as much as pay. Chile's economy contracted, with mining taking the heaviest hit. Codelco's 42,100-tonne overstatement is still unexplained, which keeps my low view on Chilean output provisional. Costs are the better news in one place: a Mexican underground AISC figure below the global median suggests the cost curve isn't rising everywhere. Gold at year-plus lows will squeeze marginal projects. Exploration is still active, with drilling spreading through Quebec, Manitoba and Ecuador, but almost all of it is years from tonnes. Harmony's fatality and new safety actions are a reminder that the industry's safety record is still a live issue.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
North America: Canada's Highland Valley dispute dominates. Federal money for Mactung and Yukon tungsten projects moves critical minerals onto a funding track, though permits still set the pace. In the US, the Hawaii ruling against the Pacific seabed plan is the first real legal test of federal mineral leasing. Utah "Alice" claim filings and new Nevada exploration notices show activity on BLM land. Mexico's cost picture is the strongest in the region.

Latin America: In Chile, small-miner reactivation after the patent law is a notable change, with reported numbers falling from 3,000 to 600 small operators. Colombia is the region's big copper bet, with AngloGold and Collective eyeing US$3.6bn across Quebradona and Guayabales. In Brazil, optimism over mining is running into a veto and El Niño, and Brasília is pushing back on the EU review of the Anglo nickel deal.

Africa: Guinea's crackdown on illegal gold is displacing tens of thousands and stalling artisanal supply, with reported stockpiling after refinery rules. Egypt's Argani is seeking control of gold mining amid backlash. In the DRC, Barrick's furlough of Congo staff over Ebola concerns shows health shutdowns can idle output as fast as a strike.

Asia-Pacific: Malaysia loosening rare-earth curbs for France shows export licensing is being traded through diplomacy. Indonesia's push for a larger state share remains policy intent without a decree.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Nickel and cobalt lose share to LFP. Ford's Michigan LFP cells for Fathom are now shipping, and LFP grid storage takes more from nickel and cobalt.
- Lithium gains from recycling rules and secondary supply, but mostly in the 2030s. Hyundai's commitment to solid-state is a long-dated lithium-metal story with uncertain timing.
- Copper's AI pull looks weaker. After the chip-shipment halt to China, I've downgraded the claim that AI data-centre demand pulls copper directly. Transformer shortages still favour electrical steel and copper grid equipment.
- Rare earths and tungsten gain from defence-linked money, and Aclara's first magnet-grade NdPr is small but real.

ON THE HORIZON:
- A signed Highland Valley deal is the swing event, with restart weeks to months later.
- The US deep-sea lease sale is due later this month, and it depends on any appeal of the Hawaii ruling.
- Trump's Asia trip, the APEC meeting in Shenzhen and the Carney–Xi meeting could bring China's antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licence terms. No dates yet.
- Codelco's explanation of the overstatement and the Chilean private-role decision.
- Indonesia's decree and Guinea's export and expulsion rules.
- What would change my view: a sustained Hormuz disruption would raise diesel and sulphur costs for leach copper and HPAL nickel before it cut metal output, which would be the biggest cost shock on the desk's list.
discussions.geologist:
INDUSTRY HEALTH:
- Copper is the fragile piece. Headlines put it below $13,000 a tonne after its worst day in over a year, as AI data-centre bets unwound. A price drop does not change this year's tonnes, but it does sharpen the surplus debate for 2027 and will make smelters and miners more cautious about new spending.
- Highland Valley is in week four. An order now bars the operator from using replacement workers, and Teck is barred from using newly promoted supervisors. Both limit how the company can keep the mine running, so they push toward a negotiated settlement, though nothing is signed.
- Gold is at year-plus lows and still falling. Exploration budgets built on gold will feel that over the winter.
- Juniors are still drilling. Inomin's nickel-magnesium results, SAGA's iron-titanium-vanadium assays, Auro's Ecuador intercept and Powermax's diamond program are the pattern: small companies are spending on mid-stage targets, not new mines.
- Chile's economy shrank, with mining taking the biggest hit. That is a macro signal that the country's copper output is not growing.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
- North America, Canada: Ottawa's up-to-C$14M offer for Mactung and federal funding for the Yukon tungsten project show that critical-minerals money is flowing. It is early-stage money, so I read it as policy and defence support rather than near-term tonnes.
- North America, US: A Hawaii federal judge ruled Trump's Pacific seabed plan violates the law. Deep-sea auctions in American Samoa and the Northern Mariana Islands are drawing environmental objections. The deep-sea lease sale later this month now depends on whether the government appeals.
- Latin America, Chile: Codelco's 42,100-tonne overstatement is still unexplained. I read the Chile low as aging pits and declining grades. Meldrum holds that view lightly until Codelco explains, and I agree with that caution.
- Latin America, Brazil and Panama: Brazil's mining optimism is running into a veto and El Niño. Panama has authorised First Quantum restart talks but has no timetable. Brazil is also pushing back on the EU review of Anglo American's nickel deal.
- Latin America, Colombia: AngloGold's $2.5bn Quebradona copper plan, with Collective eyeing US$3.6bn across Quebradona and Guayabales, is the largest new copper commitment in the set. It is years from production.
- Africa: Guinea's gold crackdown has displaced 79,000 people in Mali, according to one outlet, and deaths are rising. Egypt's Argani is seeking control of gold mining amid backlash. Artisanal disruption continues across the Sahel.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Copper: The desk's view has shifted. I had treated AI data-centre demand as a direct pull on copper. After the Nvidia chip-shipment halt to China, Dr I Simon downgraded that claim, and I think that is right. Benchmark still says data centres sustain US copper demand, so the pull is real but smaller and less certain than it looked.
- Gaining: copper and electrical steel, because transformer shortages delay grid delivery. Tungsten and antimony, through defence-linked money. Rare earths, through Malaysia loosening curbs for France and early magnet-grade output.
- Losing: nickel and cobalt, as Ford's LFP cells in Michigan and LFP grid storage take share. Mercedes' 2030 cobalt-free goal points the same way. Lead-acid is losing to sodium-ion 12V, though it trims little lithium.
- Solid-state batteries: Hyundai's "cannot give up" line means continued funding, but the timeline is long.

ON THE HORIZON:
- Highland Valley: a signed deal is the swing event. Restart follows weeks to months later.
- Deep-sea lease sale later this month, depending on any appeal of the Hawaii ruling.
- Trump's Asia trip, APEC in Shenzhen and the Carney–Xi meeting. The test is whether China publishes antimony, tungsten and rare-earth licence terms. No dates set.
- Panama–First Quantum talks: a dated restart timetable would be the first real signal.
- Chile: a Codelco explanation of the overstatement would change my reading of its grades.
discussions.strategist_reply:
Yukon, you've sharpened my view on Highland Valley. I'd treated the replacement-worker bar as a legal footnote, but you're right that it removes the operator's main way of keeping the mine running, which changes the bargaining math. Your point that a price drop doesn't change this year's tonnes is the right frame too. Where I'd push back is on 2027. Smelters chasing supply reads to me as tightness at the processing step, which usually shows first in treatment charges. I'd treat the price fall as a sentiment shock sitting on top of a concentrate squeeze, not a clean surplus signal.

I'd also keep the Chile reading a notch looser than the macro headline suggests. A shrinking economy with mining hit hardest fits your aging-pits story, but it fits equally well with the 42,100-tonne overstatement being a data problem. Until Codelco explains, I'd call it a hypothesis, which is where we already sit.

Read together, the two analyses show a desk with two markets. Defence-linked and policy-backed minerals (tungsten, antimony, rare earths, the federal money for Mactung and Yukon) are attracting state support and diplomatic bargaining. Bulk metals (copper, nickel, cobalt) face price stress, LFP substitution, and labour and health shutdowns. The Barrick Congo furlough is a useful reminder that a health event can idle output as fast as a strike, so it belongs on the same list as Highland Valley. If I had to bet on what the desk's readers will be arguing about in six months, it's whether the policy money reaches tonnes before the bulk-metal downturn reaches budgets.
discussions.geologist_reply:
Meldrum, your point that the binding constraints are people and logistics sharpens my copper view. I had treated Highland Valley mainly as a pricing and labour story, but the replacement-worker and supervisor orders show the company's options are narrowing. That is an operations problem, and it makes the signed deal a harder thing to reach.

I'd push back on two things. First, I'd keep antimony out of the "gaining" column for now. Defence money is funding projects, but the Rua write-down in New Zealand shows that a falling antimony price can still wipe out project value. Money for development and price for revenue are different signals. Second, on Mexico's below-median underground AISC, I'd treat it as one region's data point. Cost curves are set by grade, depth and ore hardness, so a good number in one district doesn't tell us the curve is flattening globally.

The pattern across both analyses is that supply is being held back more by people, permits and shutdowns than by geology, while demand is being reshaped by chemistry choices and policy money. On the Hormuz risk, I'd sharpen your point: sulphur is the HPAL reagent and sulphuric acid drives leach copper, so cost pressure would hit those routes first.

chief_sessions.opening:
GLOBAL VIEW:
The most consequential world event for mining this week is APEC in Shenzhen, where Trump is meeting Xi and, reportedly, Putin in a three-way format, with trade on the agenda. No headline mentions critical minerals. The desk's central test, whether China publishes multi-year licence terms for antimony, tungsten and rare earths, sits inside this meeting, so the link is my inference, not reporting. I expect any outcome to be framed as trade stability, with minerals detail arriving later, if at all.

The war in Ukraine keeps munitions demand high. Reports of Russia's low-cost munitions and fresh strikes on the Crimean Bridge point to sustained consumption, which supports the defence-linked tungsten and antimony money that Ottawa and Washington are now committing. This is the one part of the critical-minerals pull that does not depend on a battery cycle.

Japan's carmakers agreeing to standardise key parts and materials could narrow the battery chemistries automakers buy, which would shift the mix of nickel, cobalt and lithium. The effect is early and uncertain.

Anthropic's IPO and the Nvidia headlines feed the AI-buildout narrative that has moved copper's price. That is market sentiment, not grid demand, and I would keep it out of copper tonnage forecasts.

Myanmar's genocide verdict at the UN court has no direct mining content. Kachin state is a source of heavy rare earths, so sanctions and supply-chain scrutiny could follow over a longer horizon. This is speculative.

DESK REVIEW:
Meldrum's frame that labour, not ore, is the binding constraint is the most solid call on the desk. It holds across Highland Valley, the Barrick Congo furlough and Chile's Q3 contraction. Yukon's point that money and legal action are moving faster than tonnes is the sharpest synthesis, and Meldrum's version of it, that development finance is running ahead of tonnes, is the same insight. Both are right to keep the Codelco low provisional.

Some single-source items need more caution than the desk gave them. Mexico's below-median AISC is one district's data point, as Yukon rightly argued. The Manyar premium, the 100,000-person Mali figure and the Nunavut closure warning each rest on one report, so they should stay as context. Meldrum's "formal supply possibly rising" in Guinea is a 2028 story at the earliest, as Yukon says.

The global view changes the timing of the desk's China licence prediction. APEC puts the Trump–Xi talks in the same week as the test, so the event is closer than "no date set" suggests. Even so, a trade framework without licence terms would be a common outcome, so I hold that prediction at low confidence.

QUESTIONS FOR THE STRATEGIST:
- Smelters are chasing concentrate, and Freeport Indonesia is pre-selling 2027 copper at a premium. If your concentrate-squeeze reading is right, what should treatment and refining charges do over the next quarter, and what level would tell you the squeeze has ended?
- Defence money is backing tungsten and antimony while the Ukraine war continues. If a ceasefire came, how much of that funding would survive on civil demand alone, and which end uses would carry it?

QUESTIONS FOR THE GEOLOGIST:
- Ottawa's money for Mactung is tied to defence-driven tungsten demand. From your knowledge of skarn-hosted tungsten, what grade and continuity would Fireweed need to prove before a mine plan could be justified, and how long has that taken in comparable projects?
- If Chile's low is aging pits and falling grades, what would a Codelco mine plan show over the next two years, in terms of grade drop and tonnes, and which asset would you expect to show the decline first?

chief_sessions.strategist_answer:
On the concentrate squeeze, the cleanest signal is treatment and refining charges. Smelters are paid to take concentrate, so when concentrate is scarce, TCs fall, and when spot TCs go negative, smelters are paying for feed. Over the next quarter I expect spot TCs to stay under pressure while pre-sold tonnes such as Freeport Indonesia's 2027 volumes and the district-level shortfalls keep concentrate tight. I'd call the squeeze over when spot TCs turn clearly positive and keep rising over several weeks, and when the next annual benchmark is set above the current one. One quarterly move proves little; the trend matters. The Manyar premium rests on a single report, so I treat it as context that fits the pattern. Confidence medium.

On defence money, a ceasefire would not remove it all at once. Stockpiling and supply-security logic usually outlasts the fighting, because governments rebuild reserves. Munitions-linked demand is the part that would fall sharply: tungsten for penetrators and antimony for hardening lead in shell and ammunition alloys. Civil demand would carry much more. Tungsten carbide for cutting and mining tools is most of the metal's market. Antimony still has solar glass and some flame-retardant use, though the latter is shrinking. Rare earths would hold on EV and wind magnets. My expectation is that projects with civil offtake survive a ceasefire, while those justified only by munitions procurement get re-tested. Confidence medium-low, since no ceasefire is in the headlines and the question is hypothetical.
chief_sessions.geologist_answer:
On Mactung, skarn-hosted tungsten is a known deposit type. The scheelite forms where hot fluids reacted with limestone near intrusions. Grades are usually modest, so the mine case rests on tonnage, continuity and recovery. To justify a mine plan, Fireweed would need a resource that converts to indicated category over enough strike and depth to support a decade-plus life. It would also need a metallurgical flowsheet that reliably recovers fine-grained scheelite, and geotechnical data for a large open pit in cold northern terrain. Comparable projects have usually taken 10 to 15 years from discovery to production once permitting is included. Mactung's problem has rarely been finding the rock. It is proving the economics and getting through review. Ottawa's money helps with metallurgy and permitting data, not with the ore. The defence link changes who pays for the work, not what the rock is.

On Chile, if aging pits are the cause, a Codelco mine plan should show it in three places: head grade falling year on year at the large open pits, a rising stripping ratio as pits deepen, and flat mill throughput, so copper output falls with grade. Over two years I would expect a sustained grade decline of a few percent a year at mature pits, not a cliff. That is my field judgement, not a sourced figure. The first assets to show it would be the older open-pit complexes feeding low-grade stockpiles. El Teniente is an underground block cave with its own separate issues. The caveat matters: if the 42,100-tonne overstatement is a reserve or grade-model revision rather than a production shortfall, the mine plan will not show it directly. The answer sits in the reconciliation between the model and what the mill actually processed. That is why I keep the Codelco read provisional.

chief_sessions.opening:
GLOBAL VIEW:
The Trump, Xi and Putin summit around APEC produced a "peace declaration," and headlines disagree on what it achieved: some call it historic, others say the summit was "hijacked." The trade truce is described as "in flux." For mining, a calmer US-China trade track lowers tariff risk on copper flows, but the minerals licence terms are not in the headlines, so the desk's antimony, tungsten and rare-earth test is still open. Tighter TSMC chip curbs and warnings about AI regulation show that AI policy is moving fast, but data centres still reach mining through grids and power rather than directly.

Trump says the US will "see what happens" with Iran after January 1. That is the date to watch for Hormuz risk, which would raise diesel and sulphur costs for North American and Chilean operations before it touched metal output. Ukraine remains the source of munitions demand that holds up tungsten and antimony money. Putin has ruled out a Black Sea or energy truce, so that demand is not fading. The IMF warns global debt is nearing 100% of GDP, which tightens government budgets for critical-minerals programmes and junior financing. The Fiji drought disaster and the El Niño alert point to water and power stress in the Andes and Australia.

DESK REVIEW:
The strongest work is the shared view that labour, permits, courts and state buyers now set the pace more than geology or demand. Ford's CATL-licensed Michigan LFP output is the most concrete shift on the desk, and both analysts read it correctly. Meldrum's reading of China's premiums as a sales push, rather than a sign of shortage, is well supported.

The global view adds three things. The midterm result, which headlines describe as a Republican rout, may change the odds of a Boundary Waters moratorium and of US seabed policy, so the desk should watch Congress as well as the courts. El Niño needs to be linked to specific Andean and Australian operations. Trade-truce framing may change the Chinese premium picture.

Three predictions need tightening. The Highland Valley forecasts name "Teck," which the record does not name, so the desk should score on the operator and union as reported. The Hawaii appeal forecast gives the government a 15 December deadline, but a US government appeal can be filed within 60 days of judgment, so a filing after that date is still plausible and the call should be lower-confidence. The LME copper call has no price anchor in the record, so it cannot yet be judged on its merits.

QUESTIONS FOR THE STRATEGIST:
- If the Shenzhen trade truce holds through the year, does your reading of Chinese premiums pulling US copper strengthen or weaken, and what would make you change it?
- If the new Congress restores the Boundary Waters moratorium, does that change your timeline for North American copper-nickel supply, or only the legal route to permits?

- Which Peruvian, Chilean and Australian operations are most exposed to El Niño drought limits on water and power, and how many months after rains return would the output loss show up?
- Could El Niño-driven low water in the Panama Canal change concentrate routing from Pacific mines to Asian smelters enough to affect Cobre Panama restart planning?

chief_sessions.strategist_answer:
On the first question, a calmer trade track weakens my reading rather than strengthening it. I have been treating the pull on US copper as partly tariff-driven: metal moves to the US ahead of duties, and the US price premium draws it in. If the truce holds, the reason to front-run tariffs fades, and that flow should slow. Chinese premiums would then reflect Chinese smelter intake and domestic demand, which is a cleaner signal but a less dramatic one. Codelco's 2027 premium cut still reads as a sales push under that scenario. The headlines call the truce "in flux," so my confidence is medium.

What would change my view is a US premium over world prices that persists after tariff risk has been removed. That would suggest a structural shortage of US refined supply, not just trade timing, and I would move toward a tightening reading. A sustained Chinese premium that rises even as Codelco eases its terms would point the same way.

On Boundary Waters, Cornelius is right about the near term. The copper-nickel projects there are already stalled, so a restored moratorium would not remove supply that was about to arrive. Where I still disagree is on the timeline. A statutory withdrawal does more than change the legal route. It pushes out the date at which any project in the district could plausibly reach production, and it raises the cost of financing, because lenders price the chance that a permit never arrives. The midterm result, as headlines describe it, makes a new Congress more likely to act. I would say the restart horizon moves from uncertain to effectively open-ended, while near-term supply is unaffected. My confidence in that is medium.
chief_sessions.geologist_answer:
The Andes and Australia are not one story, so I'll take them separately.

Peru is the most exposed. Its southern highlands and the Altiplano have a history of drought-linked water stress, and its power grid leans on hydro. A dry season cuts reservoir levels, which can push up power costs and force thermal generation, so the first hit is usually cost and throughput, not metal in the ground. In my experience, a reservoir drawdown takes months to bite, so the output loss typically shows up three to nine months after the dry spell starts, and it can persist for a while after the rains return because water and power contracts and stockpiles take time to rebuild. Chile's northern copper belt is less exposed to El Niño itself because desalination and grid supply buffer it, but a hydro or Hormuz-driven diesel squeeze would hit there as cost first. Australia's eastern states are more affected by El Niño drying than the western Pilbara, so I'd watch Queensland and New South Wales for water-limited processing. I'm moderately confident on the direction and lag, and less confident on which individual mines are most at risk, because I don't have site water balances in front of me.

On the Panama Canal, I think the link is weaker than it looks. Pacific-origin concentrate bound for Asia doesn't need the canal at all, so canal drought mainly affects Atlantic-bound routes and freight costs. Cobre Panama's restart is driven by the government dispute and its own water and power needs, not by canal transit. Canal limits would raise freight and could shift smelter choices at the margin, but I would not expect them to move restart planning on their own. This is a change from how I'd have framed it if the question had been about the canal alone: the constraint that matters for Cobre Panama is political and operational first.

INDUSTRY HEALTH:
- Labour and permits, not prices, now set the pace of new supply. Highland Valley is in its fourth week with a replacement-worker order in place, and a BC court has reversed a consultation shortcut, so new tonnes are arriving later than the desk assumed.
- Gold's slide below US$3,800 squeezes juniors first while majors such as Agnico keep spending above US$3.5bn. Chinese premiums and Codelco's 2027 premium cut both look like sales pushes, not shortages.

REGIONAL TRENDS:
- North America: Canada's federal money is going to tungsten (up to C$14M for Mactung, plus funding for the Yukon project), a defence-linked policy bet that means years before tonnes. US seabed leasing is now clouded by the Hawaii ruling, and a restored Boundary Waters moratorium is a proposal whose odds the midterm result may have raised.
- Africa: Kenya's award of a large critical-minerals contract to a US consortium and Zimbabwe's lithium export-tax change with a local-sourcing mandate both show resource nationalism rising as critical minerals gain strategic value.
- Latin America: Codelco's dust-permit threat in Chile is a reminder that operating permits are live risks, and El Niño water and power stress in Peru would likely show up first as higher costs before any output loss.

TECHNOLOGY & DEMAND:
- Ford's Michigan LFP cells, built on CATL technology, take demand from nickel and cobalt and add to lithium, iron and phosphate. The shift is now production, but North American battery supply depends on a Chinese licensor.
- Electrification, which the IEA says the Hormuz crisis has accelerated, adds copper and lithium demand over time, while sodium-ion and solid-state efforts trim long-run lithium and nickel demand but remain early. Transformer shortages are the nearer copper-related bottleneck, and data centres still reach copper only through grids.

- A signed Highland Valley deal is the swing event. Restart would follow over weeks to months, so a signature alone would not add 2026 tonnes.
- The Hawaii appeal and the US deep-sea lease sale. A government appeal can be filed up to 60 days after judgment, so a filing may come after mid-December and would still be ordinary.
- Trump says the US will "see what happens" with Iran after January 1. Hormuz disruption would raise diesel and sulphur costs for North American and Chilean operations before it touched metal output.

CREATIVE ANGLES:
- Sulphur is the hidden link between Hormuz and metal supply. Sulphuric acid is used in copper solvent extraction and electrowinning in Chile, and in high-pressure acid leach nickel projects in Indonesia, so a sulphur squeeze could raise costs in both places before any sanctions or shipping limits are felt. (speculation level: medium)
- If labour is the binding constraint, the mines that gain most over the next five years may be those that automate haulage and maintenance and so need fewer hires per tonne. That would favour scale operators and could widen the gap with juniors. (speculation level: high)
- Mongolia's presidential resignation and the Mongolia–Kyrgyzstan joint-project talks could make Oyu Tolgoi's policy terms a test case for how governments reopen contracts when political leadership changes. (speculation level: medium)
